What is Sattvic sequencing?
What is the intelligent sequencing framework in yoga?
a: Sattvic sequencing seeks balanced, harmonious progression in a yoga practice, working the spine in all directions (flexion, extension, lateral flexion, rotation) and gradually building toward a peak pose before cooling down. A typical intelligent sequence follows this progression: centering and breath awareness, gentle warm-up (cat/cow, shoulder rolls, neck stretches), Surya Namaskar (sun salutations) to build heat, standing poses to develop strength and stability, balancing poses to focus the mind, backbends near the peak (warming the spine for deeper work), peak pose (the most demanding posture of the class), counterposes (forward folds, twists), inversions (after backbends, before savasana), cool-down with seated forward folds and hip openers, and finally savasana (final relaxation). Vinyasa krama means 'progressive steps'—each pose prepares the body and mind for the next, building skill, range of motion, and internal awareness gradually rather than abruptly. The peak pose model defines the entire class arc: warm-up preparatory poses target the areas needed for the peak, the peak is reached at the climax, and counterposes restore balance.

q: What is the Hatha yoga class format?
How is a Vinyasa class structured?
What is the Ashtanga yoga sequence?
What is the Iyengar method of sequencing?
What are the different yoga class formats?
How does Mysore practice work?
a: Each yoga style has a distinct class format. Hatha yoga classes typically begin with gentle warm-up, move through asanas held for longer durations (30 seconds to several minutes) with emphasis on alignment and breath, include pranayama and meditation, and end with a longer savasana. Vinyasa classes are breath-synchronized and dynamic: continuous flow from pose to pose, often set to music, with creative sequencing that may or may not follow traditional alignment rules—the emphasis is on the seamless movement between poses rather than long holds. Ashtanga yoga follows a fixed six-series sequence (primary through advanced) practiced identically each day; Mysore style allows students to move through their series at their own pace with individualized teacher adjustments. Iyengar yoga sequences are meticulously designed with specific therapeutic goals, using props extensively and holding poses for long durations while the teacher provides detailed alignment instruction—poses are sequenced to target specific body areas or health conditions.

q: What is a good morning yoga sequence?
What is a good evening yoga routine for sleep?
What are the best yoga poses for bedtime?
How do I wake up with yoga?
What is a good restorative bedtime yoga sequence?
What is the best time of day to practice yoga?
a: A morning yoga sequence should gently wake up the body, stimulate circulation, and build energy for the day: begin with breath awareness and gentle neck rolls, progress through cat/cow, sun salutations (3-5 rounds), standing poses (warrior I and II, triangle), a gentle backbend (cobra or bridge), and end with a short seated meditation or pranayama (Nadi Shodhana). An evening sequence should wind down the nervous system and prepare for sleep: start with gentle supine stretches (reclined bound angle, knees-to-chest), move through forward folds (seated forward fold, wide-legged forward fold), gentle twists (supine twist), hip openers (pigeon, happy baby), and end with legs-up-the-wall (Viparita Karani) and a long savasana or yoga nidra practice. Restorative poses using props (blankets, bolsters) are ideal for evening practice—supported child's pose, supported bridge, and reclined bound angle with full support promote deep relaxation by activating the parasympathetic nervous system.

q: How do I sequence a class for headstand?
What poses prepare for shoulderstand?
How do I work up to handstand?
What sequence builds to crow pose?
How do I prepare for wheel pose (urdhva dhanurasana)?
What are the best prep poses for backbends?
How do I sequence for Hanumanasana (splits)?
a: Peak pose sequencing builds progressively toward a specific challenging posture. For headstand (Sirsasana), warm up with dolphin pose, thread-the-needle, downward dog, forearm plank, and forearm stands at the wall before attempting headstand prep (knees to chest) and full headstand. For shoulderstand (Salamba Sarvangasana), include bridge pose to open the front body, supported shoulderstand with blankets, and plow pose (Halasana) as preparatory and counter poses. For handstand (Adho Mukha Vrksasana), build shoulder opening (dolphin, downward dog), core strength (plank variations), and wall practice (wall walks, L-stand at wall) before kicking up and eventually practicing away from the wall. For wheel pose (Urdhva Dhanurasana), sequence bridge, camel, locust, bow, upward dog, and puppy pose to open the shoulders and hip flexors before full wheel, with counterposes like knees-to-chest and gentle forward fold afterward. For splits (Hanumanasana), prepare with forward folds, lunges (crescent, half-splits), lizard pose, pigeon, and monkey pose prep with blocks under the hands, never forcing the final pose—patience and consistent practice over months to years is typical.

q: What is the structure of a yoga class?
How long should a yoga sequence be?
What is the role of counterposes in yoga sequencing?
How do I sequence inversions in a yoga class?
Should twists come before or after backbends?
How do I balance a yoga sequence?
a: A balanced yoga sequence works the body symmetrically, compensates for each major action with its opposite (counterpose), and respects the natural arcs of energy building and release. General sequencing guidelines include: warm-ups and sun salutations first to build heat, standing poses before seated poses, backbends after standing poses but before deep forward folds, inversions near the end of practice (after backbends and before savasana), and twists as counterposes for backbends and as transitional poses between categories. Inversions should be sequenced after backbends because both warm the spine, but backbends open the front body while inversions require spinal integrity and calm the nervous system—practicing inversions too early can be jarring. The fundamental principle is progressive intensity: build gradually to the most demanding work (peak or climax), then cool down symmetrically. Aim for 10-30% of practice as warm-up, 40-60% as main work (building to peak), and 20-30% as cool-down and savasana, adjusting the proportions based on the style and goals of the session.
